newsitem.title: INDIA: Britain urges India to cut bureaucratic chains.
newsitem.headline: Britain urges India to cut bureaucratic chains.

text.p: The first emissary from Britain's new Labour government to India on Thursday praised the former colony for its commitment to democracy but urged it to cut bureaucratic "chains" stifling foreign investment.
Foreign Office minister Derek Fatchett said British firms were prepared to invest greater sums to take advantage of opportunities in India's expanding economy.
But he said they often ran into daunting bureaucratic hurdles.
"There is more investment wanting to come," Fatchett told the Confederation of Indian Industry, a leading industrialist group.
"It is a frustrated investor that is wanting to come to India. It wants those bureaucratic rules to change and those chains removed."
Fatchett said India's nearly 50 years of independence had disproved those in Britain who argued Asia needs autocratic, not democratic, regimes.

"Fifty years of democracy shows that in an Asian country, democracy is dear, is important and can be maintained," Fatchett said, citing special ties between India and Britain's Labour, which was in power in 1947 when the South Asian nation won independence.
A senior British diplomat recently said nearly one billion sterling ($625 million) in British investments were being held up in what Fatchett called a "bureaucratic web".

"There is a need for the rules to be changed," the visiting British minister said, noting that firms from his country were prepared to invest in major areas such as telecommunications and power. "We are just looking for a more open system."
Foreign investment, both portfolio and direct, has risen gradually in India since it launched free-market reforms in 1991.
But foreign direct investment totalled about $2 billion in the 1996/97 fiscal year that ended on March 31, well below the government's goal of $10 billion by the end of the century.
Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, who met Fatchett on Thursday morning, told the visiting minister that India would welcome investment particularly in power, petroleum, ports and roads.
Chidambaram appealed to Britain to support India's proposal to phase out import restrictions over time, the Commerce Ministry said in a statement.
At two days of meetings in Geneva this week at the World Trade Organisation, India proposed dismantling curbs on some 2,700 goods over nine years.
India's major trading partners, including the European Union and the United States, have pressed India to phase out the restrictions, such as quotas, over two to three years.
New Delhi offered to move up the deadline from nine years, but the meeting ended inconclusively and a subsequent round of talks was set for June 30.
Fatchett was also scheduled to visit Bombay on his five-day visit ending on Sunday.
